MUJAHID:v2p502#2/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p502#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p502#2/r1.claim: Mujahid glosses the rain as drops or raindrops.

MUQATIL:30:48-50/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:30:48-50/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:30:48-50/r1.claim: God sends winds to raise clouds, divide them into pieces that pile together, and then spread them as He wills, even across distances of days' travel.

MUQATIL:30:48-50/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:30:48-50/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:30:48-50/r2.claim: Rain comes from the cloud's interior, and the people rejoice when it reaches them.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p664/r5.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p664/r5.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p664/r5.claim: God sends winds that stir clouds, spreads them across the sky as He wills, and makes them into layered pieces.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p665/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p665/r1.speaker: مجاهد
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p665/r1.claim: Mujāhid glosses al-wadq as rain, which comes through the gaps in the cloud.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p665/r2.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p665/r2.speaker: الضحاك بن مزاحم
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p665/r2.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk b. Muzāḥim recited 'from its gaps' with the variant khilalihi, referring to gaps in the cloud.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p665/r3.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p665/r3.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p665/r3.claim: People rejoice when rain reaches them, after having despaired before it came; the doubled 'before it' is an Arabic idiom, with parallels in other verses.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p342#5/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p342#5/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p342#5/r1.claim: Wadq means rain, and khilāl means the spaces between the clouds.

TAB-FULL:v18p520/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v18p520/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v18p520/r1.claim: God's winds raise or create clouds, then spread and gather them in the sky as he wills.

TAB-FULL:v18p520/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v18p520/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v18p520/r2.claim: The pronoun in “he spreads it” is masculine singular because “cloud” is treated according to its masculine form, not its plural sense.

TAB-FULL:v18p520/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v18p520/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v18p520/r3.claim: Qatada glosses spreading the cloud as gathering it.

TAB-FULL:v18p521/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v18p521/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v18p521/r1.claim: God makes the cloud into separate pieces; rain emerges from between the clouds.

TAB-FULL:v18p521/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v18p521/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v18p521/r2.claim: Qatada glosses “pieces” as separate fragments and the rain clause as rain emerging from within the cloud.

TAB-FULL:v18p521/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v18p521/r3.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
TAB-FULL:v18p521/r3.claim: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr describes four winds: one sweeps the earth, another raises and fragments clouds, a third gathers and piles them, and a fourth brings rain.

TAB-FULL:v18p521/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v18p521/r4.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v18p521/r4.claim: Mujahid glosses the rain word “wadaq” as drops.

ZAJJAJ:v4p189/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v4p189/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v4p189/r1.claim: كسفا means separate pieces of cloud; wadq is rain emerging through the cloud's gaps.

ZAJJAJ:v4p189/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v4p189/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v4p189/r2.claim: God creates clouds, revives earth, and sends winds, proving power beyond human ability and ability to resurrect the dead.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p507/r2.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p507/r2.speaker: ابن عامر
IBNMUJAHID:v1p507/r2.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir alone reads كسفا with sukūn on sīn; all others use fatḥa.

FARISI-HUJJA:v5p448#2/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p448#2/r1.speaker: ابن عامر
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p448#2/r1.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir alone has a still sīn in كسفا; the other readers open it.

FARISI-HUJJA:v5p448#2/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p448#2/r2.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p448#2/r2.claim: The opened form can be parsed like sidrah/sidr, with the same meaning as كسف; the following pronoun may refer either to the fragments or to the cloud, while the other vocalization points to the cloud alone.

THALABI:v7p305#2/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p305#2/r2.speaker: وهب بن منبه
THALABI:v7p305#2/r2.claim: He reports that the earth complained during the flood that unmeasured water gouged it; God made clouds a sieve so rain would not harm the earth.

THALABI:v7p305#2/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p305#2/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v7p305#2/r3.claim: The pronoun for the cloud follows السحاب as a masculine singular noun despite its collective plural meaning; كسفا means separate pieces.

THALABI:v7p305#2/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p305#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v7p305#2/r4.claim: He reads the rain as emerging from the cloud's middle, من خلله.

THALABI:v7p305#2/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p305#2/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v7p305#2/r5.claim: When rain reaches God's servants, they rejoice, though before its arrival they had despaired.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r1.speaker: قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r1.claim: Kisafan means pieces or fragments of cloud.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r2.speaker: يحيى بن سلام
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r2.claim: Kisafan means cloud piled one part upon another.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r3.speaker: الضحاك
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r3.claim: Kisafan may mean clouds in one sky layered beneath another.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r5.speaker: الضحاك بن مزاحم
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r5.claim: He read min khulalihi as min khalalihi.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r8.speaker: الشاعر
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p320/r8.claim: A poem about rain from clouds supports the rain interpretation.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r1.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r1.claim: Muqatil says God describes cloud-making so people will recognize His oneness: winds stir clouds and move them from where they were.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r2.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r2.claim: Muqatil says God spreads the clouds as He wills, over the distance of a day, part of a day, or several days.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r3.claim: God then makes the spread cloud into separate pieces carried by the wind; كسفا means pieces.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r4.claim: The explanation of wadq and the cloud's interior passages is given in the commentary on 24:43.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p76/r5.claim: When rain reaches the servants God chooses, they rejoice at its arrival.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:30:46-49/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:30:46-49/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:30:46-49/r3.claim: God stirs clouds from their places, spreads them or divides them into pieces, and rain emerges from their middle and cracks; those who receive it rejoice.

JISHUMI:v8p5631#2/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v8p5631#2/r6.speaker: أبو جعفر، ابن عامر
JISHUMI:v8p5631#2/r6.claim: Abu Ja'far and Ibn Amir read كسفا with still sīn as a singular piece; others vocalize it as the plural of كسفة.

JISHUMI:v8p5631#2/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v8p5631#2/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
JISHUMI:v8p5631#2/r8.claim: Ibn Abbas gives خلله without alif as a gloss for the usual خلاله; the author cautions that it may be explanation rather than a reading.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p276#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p276#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p276#2/r1.claim: God spreads the clouds as He wills, over a distance of a day, two days, or more.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p276#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p276#2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p276#2/r2.claim: Kasafan means separate pieces, wadq rain, and khilāl the clouds’ middle; people rejoice when rain reaches them.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p491/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p491/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p491/r1.claim: God sometimes spreads the cloud continuously and sometimes makes it into fragments; rain emerges from it in either arrangement.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p491/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p491/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p491/r2.claim: “The sky” means the direction or expanse above, as in 14:24.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p491/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p491/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p491/r3.claim: Rain reaching the servants means reaching their lands and territories.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p491/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p491/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p491/r4.claim: “Before it” repeats for emphasis, as in 59:17, stressing how long they had been without rain, so their despair deepened and their joy matched it.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r1.claim: Wind's stirring is moving clouds from rest and driving them onward; spreading them in the sky means dispersing them, and kisaf means pieces.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r2.speaker: الجمهور
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r2.claim: The majority read kisafan with fatḥa on the sīn; Ibn Abbas and others use the still-sīn form, both collective plurals.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r3.speaker: مكي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r3.claim: Makki says the still-sīn reading means that God makes the cloud a single piece.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r4.claim: Wadq means rain, and khilal means the spaces between the cloud's loosely joined parts; poetry illustrates wadq.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r5.speaker: الجمهور
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r5.claim: Most read min khilalihi as a plural of khalal; Ali, Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, and al-Hasan also read the collective noun min khallihi.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p341#2/r6.claim: The pronoun in khilalihi can refer to the cloud or, with the still-sīn reading, to its pieces; with fatḥa on sīn it refers only to the cloud.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r1.speaker: ابن مسعود وأبو رجاء والنخعي وطلحة بن مصرف والأعمش
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r1.claim: They read الريح in the singular rather than الرياح.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r2.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r2.claim: تثير means agitates or stirs up the cloud; God spreads it as He wills, for a day or two or less or more, and makes it into separate pieces.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r3.speaker: أبو رزين وقتادة وابن عامر وأبو جعفر وابن أبي عبلة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r3.claim: They read كسفا with a still sīn.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r4.speaker: أبو علي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r4.claim: He says the vocalized and still readings may be like سدرة and سدر, with the same meaning.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r5.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد وأبو العالية
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r5.claim: They read من خلله rather than من خلاله, as already discussed at 24:43.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r6.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p309/r6.claim: If God sends the rain to His servants, they rejoice at the rain.

QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r1.speaker: ابن محيصن وابن كثير وحمزة والكسائي
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r1.claim: These readers recite the wind in the singular; the other readers use the plural.

QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r2.speaker: أبو عمرو
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r2.claim: Winds signifying mercy are plural, while those signifying punishment are singular.

QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r3.claim: Kasaf is the plural of kisfa, meaning a piece or fragment.

QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r4.speaker: الحسن وأبو جعفر وعبد الرحمن الأعرج وابن عامر
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r4.claim: They read kasafan with a still sīn; it remains a plural of kisfa.

QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r5.claim: On the still-sīn reading, the pronoun refers to the cloud pieces; masculine agreement is acceptable because the plural has a feminine singular form.

QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r6.claim: With the other vocalization of kasaf, the following pronoun refers back to the cloud.

QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r7.speaker: الضحاك وأبو العالية وابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r7.claim: They read khilalihi as khilalihi/khilalihi with the wording khalalihi; khalal may be a plural of khilal.

QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:30:48-49/r8.claim: Al-wadq means rain, and when rain reaches the servants God wills, they rejoice at its arrival.

BAYDAWI-FULL:30:47-48/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:30:47-48/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:30:47-48/r4.claim: God's winds stir clouds, which He spreads in the sky in whatever shape or motion He wills and sometimes divides into separate masses; ابن عامر reads كسفا with a still consonant.

BAYDAWI-FULL:30:47-48/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:30:47-48/r5.speaker: ابن عامر
BAYDAWI-FULL:30:47-48/r5.claim: Ibn Amir reads كسفا with sukūn, interpreted as a lightened form, plural, or descriptive verbal noun.

BAYDAWI-FULL:30:47-48/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:30:47-48/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:30:47-48/r6.claim: Rain emerges through cloud openings; when it reaches the lands and fields of the servants God chooses, they rejoice at the coming fertility.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p277#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p277#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p277#2/r1.claim: Meccan reciters read the singular “wind”; God spreads clouds through the sky in whichever direction He wills.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p277#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p277#2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p277#2/r2.claim: “In the sky” means in its direction or expanse, as in the image of a branch in the sky.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p277#2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p277#2/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p277#2/r3.claim: Clouds may spread from the north, south, west wind, or east wind; kasfan means pieces, with readings by Yazīd and Ibn Dhakwān.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p277#2/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p277#2/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p277#2/r4.claim: God sometimes makes the clouds one continuous expanse and sometimes scattered pieces; rain emerges from their middle in either state and brings joy to affected lands.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r10.claim: When rain reaches the land God chooses, people become joyful at once; al-Akhfash treats “before it” as reinforcing “before it descends.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r11.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r11.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the repeated “before it” shows how quickly people move from despair to delight, specifying that the joy follows close upon the rain.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r12.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r12.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the repetition indicates a long drought and settled despair, making their joy proportionate to their prior need.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r5.claim: The verse about God sending winds resumes “Among His signs is that He sends winds”; the intervening sentence comforts the Prophet, promises victory, and warns unbelievers.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r6.claim: The wind's force shows divine power: delicate air precedes lightning that uproots trees and demolishes buildings, though air itself is not the agent but a voluntary actor is.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r7.claim: The same winds display wisdom by raising clouds, producing rain and crops, nourishing livestock, and distributing these benefits selectively according to God's will.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r8.claim: “Stirring” means moving the clouds, spreading means dispersing them across the horizons, and “pieces” means fragments; the pronoun in “through it” most naturally refers to clouds.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r9.speaker: وقيل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p398/r9.claim: The pronoun in “through it” may instead refer to the fragmented cloud in the reading that leaves the relevant consonant unvowelled; “sky” means the direction above.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r1.claim: The author finds the proposed implications of “before it” unobvious; the repetition serves emphasis and removes a figurative reading.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r2.speaker: قطرب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r2.claim: Quṭrub construes the words as “even before the sending,” meaning before the rain; the author rejects this as unidiomatic.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r3.speaker: وقيل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r3.claim: Another proposal supplies “before sowing,” inferred from rain and the later mention of crops turning yellow; the author says the syntax cannot support this attachment.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r4.claim: The proposed attachment to sowing fails because two prepositional phrases cannot depend on the same verb here without coordination or apposition, and rain is neither sowing nor part of it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r5.speaker: المبرد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r5.claim: Al-Mubarrad takes the pronoun to refer to clouds, but the author notes that this analysis also needs a conjunction to link the two prepositional phrases.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r6.speaker: علي بن عيسى
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p399/r6.claim: ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā interprets “before it” as before the sending; al-Kirmānī interprets it as before the glad tidings because it is paired with despair.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322#2/r1.claim: Rain emerges from within the clouds, and those who need it rejoice when it reaches them.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322/r1.claim: God sends winds that raise clouds, perhaps from the sea or wherever He wills, then spreads and enlarges them from a small cloud to fill the horizon; sometimes they arrive heavy with water, as in 7:57.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322/r2.speaker: مجاهد وأبو عمرو بن العلاء ومطر الوراق وقتادة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322/r2.claim: Mujāhid, Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, Maṭar al-Warrāq, and Qatāda say kisafan means pieces or fragments.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322/r3.speaker: الضحاك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322/r3.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says kisafan means accumulated or piled up.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322/r4.speaker: غيره
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p322/r4.claim: Another interpretation describes the clouds as black with water, dense and heavy, and close to the ground.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p323/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p323/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p323/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAmr says there are eight winds: four merciful winds—dispersing, bringing good news, sending, and spreading—and four punitive winds, two on land and two at sea.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p323/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p323/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p323/r2.claim: By God's choice, winds can bring gentleness and mercy, announce mercy, and fertilize clouds with water as a male fertilizes a female; or they can be sterile, destructive punishment, with varied directions and effects.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p323/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p323/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p323/r3.claim: A report raised to the Prophet says the wind is controlled from the second earth; a request to destroy ʿĀd with a bull-nostril-sized wind is limited to a ring's measure, linked to 51:42. Ibn Kathīr calls it rare and its Prophetic attribution objectionable, preferring it as Ibn ʿAmr's words.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p638#2/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p638#2/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p638#2/r1.claim: Rain reaching a land or person God chooses is a sheer favor, not something owed; the recipients owe worship, gratitude, and submission, yet they quickly rejoice in the hoped-for harvest despite possible setbacks.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p638#2/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p638#2/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p638#2/r2.claim: The people rejoice at once because they anticipate the beneficial effects of rainfall, such as fertility, moisture, and softness.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p638/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p638/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p638/r1.claim: The plural reading riyaḥ, used by most reciters rather than Ibn Kathir, Hamza, and al-Kisaʾi, highlights the varied winds God can use to raise clouds.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p638/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p638/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p638/r2.claim: God first makes the wind raise clouds that did not exist, then attributes spreading and dividing the clouds to himself to show that no natural force acts independently.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p638/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p638/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p638/r3.claim: The clouds' varied distances and forms show that God alone freely chooses how to spread them, without nature or another cause controlling him.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p638/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p638/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p638/r4.claim: God makes clouds into separate pieces, leaving openings through which rain can descend; al-wadq is abundant, continuous rain emerging through the clouds in either joined or divided states.

DURR-FULL:v6p498/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p498/r2.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v6p498/r2.claim: Mujahid glosses the winds’ glad tidings and God’s mercy as rain, the ships as vessels at sea, and seeking God’s bounty as trade by ship.

DURR-FULL:v6p498/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p498/r4.speaker: السدي
DURR-FULL:v6p498/r4.claim: Al-Suddi describes wind gathering cloud from the sky’s horizons, spreading it, water flowing over it, and rain falling from it.

DURR-FULL:v6p498/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p498/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v6p498/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says winds carry water from clouds, which yield rain in heavy but scattered streams like a milking camel.

DURR-FULL:v6p498/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p498/r6.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v6p498/r6.claim: Qatada says God gathers the cloud and makes it into pieces.

DURR-FULL:v6p500/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p500/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v6p500/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says cloud pieces are stacked atop one another, rain comes through them, and al-wadaq means rain; Mujahid calls it drops of rain, while al-Dahhak takes cloud pieces as one heaven beneath another and mublisīn as despairing.

BURSEVI:v7p37#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p37#2/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p37#2/r7.claim: The winds are winds of mercy, such as the east wind; إثارة means scattering clouds and raising them, and clouds is a generic noun usable for one or many.

BURSEVI:v7p38/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p38/r1.speaker: المفردات
BURSEVI:v7p38/r1.claim: Al-Mufradat derives clouds from dragging, either because wind drags them or because they carry water.

BURSEVI:v7p38/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p38/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p38/r2.claim: Winds spread and dislodge clouds from their places; the action is attributed to the winds as its cause although God is the true agent.

BURSEVI:v7p38/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p38/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p38/r3.claim: God spreads the clouds as one connected mass in whichever direction and speed He wills, or separates them into pieces; كسفا is plural of a cloud fragment.

BURSEVI:v7p38/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p38/r4.speaker: الراغب
BURSEVI:v7p38/r4.claim: Al-Raghib says الودق may mean dust-like material within rain and may also denote rain itself; الخلل means a gap and جمعه is خلال.

BURSEVI:v7p38/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p38/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p38/r5.claim: Rain emerges by divine command from the cloud's holes and openings both when it is joined and when divided.

BURSEVI:v7p38/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p38/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p38/r6.claim: Clouds are likened to a sieve so that rain does not damage the earth.

BURSEVI:v7p38/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p38/r7.speaker: وهب بن منبه
BURSEVI:v7p38/r7.claim: Wahb reports that during the Flood the earth complained that unmeasured water had scratched and gouged it; God promised to make the clouds a sieve for rain.

BURSEVI:v7p38/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p38/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p38/r8.claim: When God sends rain to chosen servants, they immediately rejoice at fertility and the end of drought; the pronoun refers to rain.

ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r1.claim: This resumes the earlier mention of winds: they stir and spread clouds, then spread them as one mass or make pieces, according to God’s will.

ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r2.claim: ‘In the sky’ means in its direction, not inside the sky in the ordinary sense; clouds may travel, stop, and cover all or part.

ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r3.speaker: ابن عامر
ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r3.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads kusfan with still sīn; it may be shortened, plural of kusfah, verbal noun, or description with an omitted ‘possessing pieces.’

ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r4.claim: Wadq is rain emerging through cloud openings in connected and fragmented states; the pronoun refers to the masculine collective noun ‘cloud.’

ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r5.claim: On the still-sīn reading, the pronoun might refer to kasf itself, but al-Ālūsī calls this unsound.

ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v21p52#2/r6.claim: Rain reaching lands of whichever servants God wills brings sudden joy at fertile abundance; the bāʾ is transitive.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r1.claim: Ithāra means stirring dust or air until it leaves its place; clouds arise as winds create atmospheric moisture through interaction of heat and cold.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r2.claim: Basṭ means spreading, and the sky here is the upper atmosphere where clouds form.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r3.claim: Kayfa is an adverbial substitute for the verbal noun of yabṣuṭu, meaning God spreads the cloud in whatever manner He wills; treating it as conditional is incorrect.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r4.speaker: الجمهور
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r4.claim: The majority read kisafan with kasra then fatḥa as the plural of kisf; kisfa also means a piece or fragment.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r5.claim: The cloud is spread broadly and darkens the sky in one state, then appears as separate cloud masses in another; this variation manifests God's vast power.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r6.claim: The address in ‘you see’ is general; wadq means rain, and its channels are the gaps within either form of cloud.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p121/r7.claim: People's joy when rain falls and despair when it stops recalls God's mercy and shows His control over changing human and cloud responses.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p56/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p56/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v21p56/r5.claim: Athārū is coordinated with kānū and derives from stirring or turning something settled; 30:48 also uses athāra for winds moving clouds.

TABATABAI:30:48-49/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:30:48-49/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:30:48-49/r1.claim: This is the third proof from God's acts, chiefly aimed at establishing resurrection; since denial of resurrection undermines law and religion, the Prophet is directed toward those ready to believe.

TABATABAI:30:48-49/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:30:48-49/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:30:48-49/r2.claim: Wind stirs and spreads clouds, God stretches them in the upper air as He wills and divides them into masses, and rain falls through their gaps to give life to people, animals, and plants.

TABATABAI:30:48-49/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:30:48-49/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:30:48-49/r3.claim: Ethāra is stirring and spreading, sky is whatever is above and shelters, kasaf is plural for pieces, wadq is rain, and khilāl are openings.

ASAD-NOTES:30:42#n44/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:30:42#n44/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:30:42#n44/r1.claim: The winds symbolize spiritual life and hope, as in verse 46; Asad therefore adds this sense in translation.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:30:46/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:30:46/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:30:46/r1.claim: Ordinary natural events are signs of God’s unity and power; after verse 41’s environmental damage, the passage shows nature’s God-given order as evidence, though humans can disrupt it, linking winds, ships, clouds, rain, and revived earth to other Quran passages.

QIRAAT-ER:30:48:16#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:30:48:16#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:30:48:16#1/r1.claim: With sukūn, kisfan means one piece or slab; with fatḥa, kisafan means fragments.

QIRAAT-ER:30:48:4#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:30:48:4#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:30:48:4#1/r1.claim: Singular wind presents a unified force, whereas plural winds suggests diverse directional winds.

STUDYQURAN:30:48/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:30:48/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:30:48/r1.claim: The Quran uses the plural “winds” ten times, each time expressing God’s mercy, including the cited passages.

STUDYQURAN:30:48/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:30:48/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:30:48/r2.claim: The singular “wind” usually conveys God’s wrath and punishment.

STUDYQURAN:30:48/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:30:48/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:30:48/r3.claim: The distinction may reflect a view that south, east, and north winds bring mercy, while the west wind brings punishment and destruction.

STUDYQURAN:30:48/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:30:48/r4.speaker: IK
STUDYQURAN:30:48/r4.claim: Kisaf, translated “fragments,” can also mean “piled up.”

STUDYQURAN:30:48/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:30:48/r5.speaker: IK
STUDYQURAN:30:48/r5.claim: Those receiving rain may have despaired from need before the rain relieved them.

STUDYQURAN:30:48/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:30:48/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:30:48/r6.claim: Alternatively, people may have feared a violent storm when the winds arose, then felt relief when only rain came.

STUDYQURAN:30:intro/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:30:intro/r12.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:30:intro/r12.claim: After calling people to upright religion, the sūrah contrasts believers and disbelievers and returns to reflection on God’s signs.
